decks.module: Checking brakes, lights, glass and tires
decks.domain: Before you drive: vehicle, belts, phones, insurance

cards.front: Which brake warning signs send a car to a mechanic, and why do brakes matter so much?
cards.back: Only the brakes stop the car, so noise, odd smells, a floor bound pedal or pulling aside all send the car to a mechanic.

cards.front: Which steering problems need a mechanic, and how soon?
cards.back: Steering that fights back or answers late belongs in a mechanic bay before the next drive.

cards.front: What do repeated bouncing or wrestling the wheel after bumps point to?
cards.back: Repeated bouncing or wrestling the wheel after bumps points at worn shocks and a mechanic visit.

cards.front: Which lights must work as seen from outside, and what headlight problem needs fixing?
cards.back: Signals, brake, tail and head lights must all work as seen from outside, and a skewed headlight that blinds others needs fixing.

cards.front: How should you prepare the windows, wipers and windshield before driving?
cards.back: Strip snow, ice and frost from every window, keep wipers and washer fluid ready, clean glass inside too, and replace cracked windshields.

cards.front: What is the horn for?
cards.back: The horn serves only as a warning to others, though that warning can save a life.

cards.front: How should you check tire pressure, and how often should you inspect tires for wear and damage?
cards.back: Worn or bald tires lengthen stopping distance and make wet turns harder, so check tire pressure with a gauge against the owner's manual or driver's door jamb recommendation, and inspect tires for wear and damage monthly and before long road trips.

cards.front: How does the penny test work?
cards.back: For the penny test, place Lincoln's head into one of the grooves where tread looks lowest: if any part of Lincoln's head is covered by tread, tread depth is safe, whereas lower tread greatly reduces road grip in adverse conditions.

cards.front: In the penny test, what does a covered part of Lincoln's head mean versus tread below that level?
cards.back: In the penny test, having any part of Lincoln's head covered by tread shows safe tread depth, whereas tread below that mark means road grip in adverse conditions is sharply reduced.
cards.memory_hook: Head covered: safe; lower: less grip

decks.domain: Before you drive: vehicle, belts, phones, insurance

cards.front: Which maintenance schedule do drivers owe their cars, and why?
cards.back: Drivers owe their cars the owner manual maintenance schedule, since neglected cars strand and crash their owners.

cards.front: What can a sick engine do, and how do you guard against it?
cards.back: A sick engine may fade, stall, drink fuel and foul air, even dying mid road, so keep its manual service dates.

cards.front: Why is leaky exhaust dangerous, and what precautions does the manual give?
cards.back: Leaky exhaust can kill riders swiftly, so never idle in a shut garage, crack a window during long idles, and test the system on schedule.
cards.memory_hook: never idle in a shut garage

cards.front: How long does a failed emissions check give you to repair and retest?
cards.back: A failed emissions check grants sixty days to repair and retest the vehicle.

cards.front: How does fuel burning affect the climate, and how can buyers fight it?
cards.back: Fuel burning feeds climate change with carbon dioxide, which buyers fight by shopping emissions and economy ratings and by driving thriftily.

cards.front: What can aftermarket tint and lighting swaps do?
cards.back: Aftermarket tint and lighting swaps can break legal equipment standards.

cards.front: What does a registered car need, and what happens after an insurance lapse?
cards.back: Registered cars need unbroken insurance, lapses draw a DMV warning offering a compliance pact and fine, silence suspends the registration, and bare registration bans the road.

cards.front: What comes first after an insurance lapse, and what follows if the notice is ignored?
cards.back: An insurance lapse first buys a warning with a compliance pact and fine, but ignoring that notice kills the registration and grounds the car.

decks.domain: Before you drive: vehicle, belts, phones, insurance

cards.front: How should the seat and mirrors be set before moving?
cards.back: Set seat and mirrors before moving: rearview frames the back glass, side mirrors the flanks, confirmed by leaning forward to glimpse the car side.

cards.front: Why should loose cargo be stowed and the floors cleared?
cards.back: Stow loose cargo and clear the floors so nothing flies in a stop or wedges beneath the brake pedal.

cards.front: Who must be belted or restrained before rolling, and do airbags excuse bare belts?
cards.back: Connecticut orders belts on every occupant plus proper child restraints before rolling, and airbags never excuse bare belts against side, rear or rollover hits.

cards.front: What do two part belts and automatic shoulder belts require?
cards.back: Two part belts demand both lap and shoulder straps, and auto shoulder belts still need the manual lap buckle against sliding out.

cards.front: Which areas do airbags guard, and when do belts stay mandatory?
cards.back: Airbags guard the wheel, dash and windshield only, so belts stay mandatory for side, rear and rollover blows and for holding the driver behind the wheel.

cards.front: What does each unbelted driver and each unbelted rider face?
cards.back: An unbelted driver and an unbelted rider each draw their own citation and a seventy five dollar fine.

cards.front: Which riders must every driver see belted, and what does each bare rider earn?
cards.back: Every driver must see seven to sixteen year old riders belted, every occupant must wear one, and each bare rider earns a citation.

cards.front: Is a belt ticket shared by the driver and passenger, or issued separately?
cards.back: Driver and passenger belt tickets land separately: each bare occupant earns a personal citation and fine rather than one shared ticket.

decks.domain: Before you drive: vehicle, belts, phones, insurance

cards.front: How must babies and toddlers ride, by age and weight?
cards.back: Babies under two or under thirty pounds ride rear facing with a five point harness, and tots of two to five or under forty pounds ride rear or forward facing still harnessed.

cards.front: Which seats do older children use, how are age and weight ties settled, and where may a rear facing seat never sit?
cards.back: Kids of five to eight or forty to sixty pounds use a harness or booster, older bigger kids a booster or belt, age weight ties break toward stricter seats, and rear facing seats never face a live front airbag.

cards.front: What separates the rear facing only tier from the forward facing harnessed tier?
cards.back: Under two years or under thirty pounds means rear facing only, while two to five years or under forty pounds opens the forward facing harnessed seat.

cards.front: Which seats suit children of five to eight and older bigger kids, and what decides split cases?
cards.back: Five to eight years or forty to sixty pounds allows a harness or booster, eight plus years with sixty plus pounds allows a booster or plain belt, and split cases always take the stricter seat.

decks.module: Seat belt myths and crash numbers
decks.domain: Before you drive: vehicle, belts, phones, insurance

cards.front: How fast do belts release, how common are fire and sinking traps, and what does a belt do for escape?
cards.back: Belts release in under a second, fire and sinking traps are rare, and a belted rider stays conscious to escape.

cards.front: Why is staying belted inside better than ejection, and which way do side struck riders slide?
cards.back: Staying belted inside beats ejection into traffic, and side struck riders slide toward the impact rather than away.

cards.front: How close to home do road deaths strike, and on which streets?
cards.back: More than half of road deaths strike within twenty five miles of home, many on streets posted below forty five miles per hour.

cards.front: What does a head on hit at twenty five miles per hour compare to?
cards.back: A twenty five mile per hour head on hit matches a full speed bicycle into a wall or a three story sidewalk dive, far past bracing.

cards.front: Which two numbers disprove short trip myths?
cards.back: Short trip myths die on two numbers: deaths cluster within twenty five miles of home, and a twenty five mile per hour crash hits like a wall or a three story fall.

decks.domain: Before you drive: vehicle, belts, phones, insurance

cards.front: Where and when are handheld phones banned, and who may go hands free?
cards.back: Handheld phones and mobile devices stay off on public highways even in traffic stops, parked shoulders allow use, adults may go hands free only, and sixteen and seventeen year olds may use nothing at all.

cards.front: Does a car halted by traffic or signals count as operating for the phone ban?
cards.back: A car halted by traffic or signals still counts as operating for the phone ban, while a car parked safely roadside frees the driver to call.

cards.front: How do the phone rules for adults differ from the rules for sixteen and seventeen year olds?
cards.back: Adults may talk hands free behind the wheel, but sixteen and seventeen year olds may touch no phone or device whatever, hands free included.

cards.front: Which calls and which users are exempt from the handheld phone ban?
cards.back: In an emergency, a driver of any age may use a cell phone or mobile electronic device to call police or fire departments, an ambulance service, a hospital, a health clinic, a physician's office, or an emergency response operator, while peace officers, firefighters, and ambulance drivers eighteen or older may use handheld devices.

cards.front: What does a teen phone ticket count as, and what follows from it?
cards.back: A teen phone ticket counts as a moving violation, convicts under eighteen into a license suspension, and feeds the retraining tally.

cards.front: How does an emergency call differ from a teen social call under the phone rules?
cards.back: Emergency calls to responders and clinics stay legal at any age, yet a teen social call draws a moving violation, a suspension on conviction, and a retraining mark.

recaps.module: Checking brakes, lights, glass and tires

recap_hooks.text: Brakes, steering and shocks that misbehave all go to a mechanic, and every outside light must work.
Keep the glass clear, check tires for wear and damage monthly, and in the penny test any covered part of Lincoln's head means safe tread.
Follow the owner manual service schedule, and never let the engine idle in a shut garage.
A failed emissions check leaves sixty days to repair and retest.
An insurance lapse brings a DMV warning first, and ignoring it suspends the registration.
Set the seat and mirrors and stow loose cargo before the car moves.
Every occupant buckles up, airbags never replace belts, and each unbelted person gets a separate citation and fine.
The youngest children ride rear facing in a five point harness, and split age and weight cases take the stricter seat.
A rear facing seat never faces a live front airbag.

recaps.module: Seat belt myths and crash numbers

recap_hooks.text: More than half of road deaths happen within twenty five miles of home, and a twenty five mile per hour crash hits like a three story fall.
Belts release in under a second and keep riders inside the car and conscious to escape.
Handheld phones stay off even when stopped in traffic, adults may only go hands free, and sixteen and seventeen year olds may use nothing.
Emergency calls are allowed at any age, but a teen phone ticket is a moving violation.
